sittings.bodyEn: Project 1 proves you measure model output with automatic checks, not guesswork. You score three versions of a WeUseAI support prompt on thirty real messages. Five code checks decide each reply: json, intent, escalate, indonesian, and safe. Roles that care include 提示词设计 and 对话质检. Honest limit: pretty sample replies without a fixed score sheet will not survive an interview.

terms.hook: If they say this, they mean score results with fixed checks, not vibes.

sittings.bodyEn: Create one repo, init git, and make a Python 3.12 venv — older Mac Pythons break later MCP work. Install the shared packages until every import works. Put LLM_BASE_URL, LLM_API_KEY, LLM_MODEL, and EMBED_MODEL in environment variables only. Route every project through one small chat helper so switching providers is four lines. Honest limit: keys in source files will get you rejected before your scores matter.

terms.hook: If they say this, they mean a Hangzhou-friendly hosted Qwen API.

sittings.bodyEn: Collect thirty real messages, strip personal data, and include angry, unclear, and mixed-language cases. Label intent and needs_human before you see model output. Save the rows as a CSV you will reuse after every prompt change. Read the five checkers before any run so you cannot bend them later. Honest limit: an easy-only set will make every prompt look finished.

terms.hook: If they say this, they mean inspect replies against fixed rules.

sittings.bodyEn: Run version 1 as a weak one-line prompt and read every failure. For version 2, change only one thing — intents and escalate rules — then compare. Version 3 is the full six-part prompt plus examples. Fill a real score table out of 150 and optionally rerun on a smaller model for cost. Honest limit: changing labels, rules, and examples at once destroys the story of what helped.

terms.hook: If they say this, they mean hand the case to a human agent.

sittings.bodyEn: Done means thirty labeled messages, three prompt files, and a scoring script anyone can rerun. The table shows your real totals, not placeholders. A one-page write-up covers task, data, five checks, remaining failures, and cost per 1,000 messages. The same numbers appear under personal projects on your CV. Honest limit: if a classmate cannot reproduce the table, it is not done.

terms.hook: If they say this, they mean finished work with numbers on a CV.

sittings.bodyEn: Never invent table cells or round scores up to look better. Never commit API keys. Pin package versions when something breaks instead of guessing. Spend leftover time on a ninety-second story with real blanks filled in. Honest limit: eight hours is enough only if labeling and failure reading get calendar space.
Pick the claim that matches measuring output instead of guessing. Ignore answers about training Transformers or replacing MCP.
sittings.prompt: What does the prompt-evaluation sheet prove?
choices: That you can train a Transformer from scratch in PyTorch
That you measure model output with automatic checks, not guesswork
That fine-tuning always beats a good prompt
That MCP servers replace function calling

sittings.bodyEn: Project 1 runs a fixed set of automatic checks on every model output. Count those checks, not the thirty messages. The five names are json, intent, escalate, indonesian, and safe.
sittings.prompt: How many automatic checks does Project 1 run on each model output?
